content: The scalp is the anatomical region that is bordered by the face at the front and the neck at the sides and back. It is composed of five distinct layers, which can be remembered using the mnemonic SCALP: 1. Skin: The outermost layer of the scalp is the skin, which supports the growth of hair. This layer is highly vascularized, meaning it has an abundant supply of blood vessels. It is prone to conditions such as dandruff and cutis verticis gyrata, a rare disorder characterized by folds and ridges in the scalp. 2. Connective Tissue: Beneath the skin lies a thin layer of fat and fibrous connective tissue. This layer provides structural support to the skin. 3. Aponeurosis (Galea Aponeurotica): This is a tough, dense fibrous tissue layer that connects the frontalis muscle at the front of the scalp to the occipitalis muscle at the back. It plays a key role in the movement of the scalp. 4. Loose Areolar Connective Tissue: This layer allows for easy separation between the upper three layers and the pericranium. It is the layer through which the scalp can be torn off in cases of scalping injuries. It also serves as a surgical plane in craniofacial and neurosurgical procedures. This layer is sometimes referred to as the Danger Zone because infections can easily spread through it to the emissary veins, which drain into the cranial cavity. The loose areolar tissue is composed of randomly arranged collagen type I and type III fibers, is highly vascularized, and contains a significant amount of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in its extracellular matrix. 5. Pericranium: This is the periosteum, or the connective tissue layer that covers the bones of the skull. It provides nourishment to the underlying bone and has the capacity to repair it. During surgical procedures such as craniotomy, the pericranium can be lifted to allow access to the skull. Blood Supply The scalp receives its blood supply from four pairs of arteries, two of which originate from the internal carotid artery and two from the external carotid artery: Internal Carotid Artery: The supratrochlear artery supplies the midline of the forehead. The supraorbital artery supplies the lateral forehead and the scalp up to the vertex. External Carotid Artery: The superficial temporal artery provides frontal and parietal branches to supply much of the scalp. The occipital artery supplies the posterior region of the scalp. Innervation The scalp is innervated by several nerves: The supratrochlear nerve and supraorbital nerve, both branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, provide sensation to the forehead and anterior scalp. The greater occipital nerve (C2) innervates the posterior scalp up to the vertex. The lesser occipital nerve (C3) supplies the area behind the ear. The zygomaticotemporal nerve, a branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, innervates the hairless temple region. The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, provides sensation to the lateral scalp. Role in Aesthetics The scalp plays a significant role in facial aesthetics. Androgenic alopecia, commonly known as male pattern baldness, is a frequent concern among men. Treatment options include medications such as finasteride or hair transplantation, though the success of these treatments varies. With aging, the scalp may become heavy and loose, leading to a low, heavy, and deeply lined forehead. A brow lift procedure can address these aesthetic concerns by elevating the forehead and improving its appearance. Pathology The scalp is a common site for the development of various tumors, including: Epidermoid cysts Pilar cysts Actinic keratosis, which can progress to squamous cell carcinoma Basal cell carcinoma Merkel cell tumors
